p.x:
My idol is a Thai badminton player called Ploy. She was born in a small village in the north. Her family was not rich, and she was an ordinary girl. But she loved badminton and practised very hard every day after school.
When she was sixteen, she won her first big award. Now she is famous all over the world. Last year, she won a gold medal at a big competition.
I remember the day I met her at a shopping mall. She was very kind and friendly. She said, "Never give up!" I want to be like her. My grandfather says that even after famous people die, the world remembers them because of their hard work.

Dr Anong Saelim is a renowned Thai scientist, although she grew up in a poor family in Isan. During her childhood, she helped her parents in the rice fields, but she always found time to read. Her teachers noticed that she was very talented at maths and science.
With great courage, she moved to Bangkok alone at the age of eighteen to study at university. Life was hard, and she had to make many sacrifices: she worked in a restaurant at night to pay for her studies. But she was determined, and she overcame every difficulty.
Today, she is one of the most influential scientists in Asia. Her research on clean water has helped millions of people, and some say she could win the Nobel Prize one day. Many people admire her because she is so dedicated to her work.
Dr Anong's rise to fame was not an overnight success; it took thirty years of hard work. She is also an activist who encourages girls to study science. "Being a role model is an honour," she says. "My greatest achievement is seeing young people follow their dreams." She has written a memoir about her life, and she happily signs her autograph for students. Unlike some controversial celebrities, she avoids the paparazzi and fame does not interest her.

History is full of people who became renowned for their achievements, yet the path to recognition is rarely straightforward. Some, like child prodigies in music or mathematics, are recognised early. Others work for decades in obscurity, and a few receive recognition only after their death. The painter Vincent van Gogh, for example, sold very few paintings during his lifetime; his posthumous fame is now enormous.
Many of the most admired figures share a story of rising from humble beginnings and facing adversity. Such stories are inspiring, but psychologists warn that they can also be misleading. For every successful person who overcame difficult circumstances, many equally talented people did not succeed, often because of factors beyond their control, such as illness, lack of opportunity or simple bad luck.
The nature of fame has also changed. In the past, prominent figures were typically political leaders, eminent scientists or great artists. Today, social media allows ordinary people to gain millions of followers almost overnight, sometimes for skills that seem trivial to older generations. Critics argue that this has created a culture that values visibility over achievement.
Yet many people still choose role models for their character rather than their fame: the trailblazer who opened doors for others, the philanthropist who used their wealth to help communities, or the teacher who changed students' lives. Perhaps the greatest tribute we can pay to such people is not to imitate their success, but to share their values.
